title: Linear CONGEST lower bound with logarithmic LOCAL complexity
formal: Do there exist a fixed maximum degree \(\Delta\), a locally checkable labeling problem \(\Pi\) on all connected simple graphs of maximum degree at most \(\Delta\), and a deterministic LOCAL algorithm solving \(\Pi\) in \(O(\log N)\) rounds, such that every randomized CONGEST algorithm solving \(\Pi\) with global failure probability at most \(1/N\) requires \(\Omega(N)\) worst-case rounds? The common size parameter \(N\ge2\) is known to every vertex, and each algorithm must meet its guarantee on every input with at most \(N\) vertices. Use the models and quantifiers below; no additional promise on the graph or input labels is allowed.

why: Local verifiability limits what a problem can demand of a global solution, but it need not make that solution easy to construct with short messages. A logarithmic-versus-linear separation would show that bandwidth can cause a near-global delay even when graph distances and local verification permit a much faster solution. The requirement of one total bounded-degree LCL rules out explanations based on an arbitrary promise or an output whose size grows with the network.
status_note: Explicitly posed in DISC 2021. Bounded primary-source checks through 2026-09-15 found the existing sublinear CONGEST lower bound and 2026 results on LCL formalisms, but no resolution of the logarithmic deterministic LOCAL versus linear randomized CONGEST target. This is an individual model review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

progress.text: Balliu et al. state the linear-separation question on printed page 8:4, define the models on pages 8:6–8:7, and give a deterministic logarithmic LOCAL upper bound with randomized \(\Omega(\sqrt N/\log^2 N)\) CONGEST hardness in the full version’s Section 6.
Cruciani et al. introduce their result on equivalence of LCL formalisms. The author page subsequently lists it for DISC 2026; the result does not give the requested linear bandwidth separation.

importance.reason: A fundamental bandwidth-versus-locality separation question for the broad and precisely defined LCL framework. Closing the logarithmic-to-linear gap would identify an extreme resource separation even when solutions are locally checkable and degrees and labels are constant.

sentences: An LCL specifies legal output labels by a finite list of constant-radius neighborhoods.
The question asks for one problem that is solvable in logarithmic deterministic LOCAL time but needs linear randomized CONGEST time.
Both models communicate along the same bounded-degree graph, while CONGEST restricts each message to logarithmically many bits.
Such a result would isolate an extreme cost of bandwidth despite local verifiability of solutions.
The card requires all connected inputs without additional promises and states the identifiers, private randomness and global error convention explicitly.

definitions: An LCL specification consists of an integer \(\Delta\ge1\), a radius \(r\ge1\), finite nonempty input and output alphabets \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{in}},\Sigma_{\mathrm{out}}\), and a finite list \(\mathcal C\) of permitted rooted radius-\(r\) neighborhoods with both input and output labels on every incidence \((v,e)\) where vertex \(v\) is an endpoint of edge \(e\). A radius-\(r\) neighborhood is the subgraph induced by vertices at graph distance at most \(r\) from its root; labels on incidences of its included edges are retained. An output is legal if every such rooted neighborhood is isomorphic to one in \(\mathcal C\), preserving roots and input/output labels. Identifiers, the parameter \(N\), and communication-port numbers are not part of this legality test. The problem must have a legal output for every connected simple graph of degree at most \(\Delta\) with every assignment of input incidence labels. All parts of the specification are fixed independently of the input size. Each vertex is a processor; each incident edge has a distinct local port number in \(\{1,\ldots,\deg(v)\}\), chosen arbitrarily. Initially a vertex knows only \(N\), its degree, its ports and its own incidence input labels, together with its identifier in the deterministic model. Communication uses only graph edges. In one synchronous round each vertex sends a separate message to each neighbor using only its state before the round; messages arrive at its end. LOCAL permits any finite message length. A CONGEST algorithm has a fixed integer bandwidth constant \(\beta\ge1\) and sends one padded string of at most \(\lceil\beta\log_2(N+2)\rceil\) bits per directed edge per round; the bound includes all protocol data. Local computation and memory are uncharged but finite and terminating, and each algorithm has one finite program independent of \(N\). The deterministic LOCAL algorithm must work for every injective assignment of identifiers from \(\{1,\ldots,N^3\}\). The randomized CONGEST algorithm receives no identifiers and uses mutually independent fair private random bits at the vertices, with some finite computable bound \(h_B(N)\) on the number used per vertex. It must finish within a deterministic round bound on every coin sequence, and for each graph, port assignment and input labeling, the probability that all output neighborhoods are legal is at least \(1-1/N\). Outputs are labels on the processor’s own incidences. Let \(t_B(N)\) be the maximum rounds until all vertices output, over all such inputs of size at most \(N\) and all coins. The claimed separation means there is one LOCAL algorithm and constant \(C\) with round bound \(C\log_2(N+2)\) for every \(N\), and, for every correct randomized CONGEST algorithm \(B\) with any fixed \(\beta\), there exist \(c_B>0,N_B\) such that \(t_B(N)\ge c_BN\) for all integers \(N\ge N_B\). The constants in the lower bound may depend on \(B\) and its bandwidth, but \(\Pi,\Delta,r\) and the alphabets are fixed first.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean either establishing this existence statement or proving its negation. An affirmative answer must provide the complete finite LCL specification, prove total solvability, give the deterministic logarithmic-round LOCAL algorithm, and prove the linear worst-case CONGEST lower bound against every randomized algorithm in the stated error and bandwidth model. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a lower bound on a promised subfamily without a total LCL on all bounded-degree inputs, or an \(\Omega(N/\log N)\) bound does not meet the target. A negative answer must exclude every qualifying LCL, not merely the existing construction. No numerical tolerance replaces the required asymptotic bounds.

context_blocks.text: The 2021 paper establishes equality between LOCAL and CONGEST complexities for LCLs on trees, and a separation on general bounded-degree graphs. Its explicit open question asks whether the gap can extend from logarithmic LOCAL time to linear CONGEST time. The statement here retains that stronger endpoint rather than counting any superpolylogarithmic gap as success.

The authors’ known example has an \(O(\log N)\) deterministic LOCAL algorithm and an \(\Omega(\sqrt N/\log^2 N)\) randomized CONGEST lower bound. It establishes a genuine bandwidth effect but falls short of the linear lower bound requested here.

Arbitrary input labels and every connected graph up to the degree bound are part of the problem domain. Restricting the network to a specially chosen family would remove a central part of the LCL requirement. The graph size, identifiers and random bits also cannot be encoded into a growing output alphabet, since the specification must be finite and fixed.

The source defines randomized algorithms without identifiers and deterministic algorithms with polynomially bounded identifiers. It also requires a deterministic round bound and high global success probability. The card fixes those conventions explicitly; the paper’s discussion explains that randomized identifier generation can bridge the common identifier conventions, with a change in failure probability.

Cruciani, Das, Raevskaya and Suomela’s 2026 work studies robustness of LCL definitions under local reductions. Its stated translation results concern formalism and local simulation overhead, rather than a logarithmic-versus-linear LOCAL–CONGEST theorem. They do not resolve this target.
